entry: Process of Spanish conquest and settlement in the Americas, beginning in 1493. It started on the Caribbean island of [[Hispaniola]] after a 1492 voyage by Genoese mariner [[Christopher Columbus]] under license from Queen [[Isabella I of Castile]]. Religion played an important role, as indigenous peoples were brought into the [[Catholic Church]] peacefully or by force. An estimated 1.86 million Spaniards settled in the Americas between 1492 and 1832. The indigenous population fell by an estimated 80% in the century and a half after Columbus's voyages, primarily through infectious diseases, while forced labor and slavery were used for resource extraction. The Spanish American wars of independence in the early 19th century led to the secession of most of Spanish America. [[Cuba]], [[Puerto Rico]] and the [[Philippines]] stayed under Spanish rule until they were lost to the United States in 1898, after the [[Spanish–American War]].

headword: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire
sort_key: spanish conquest of the aztec empire
entry: Campaign in which Spanish forces overthrew the Aztec Empire, 1519–1521. [[Hernán Cortés]] led a small army of European soldiers and a large allied army of Indian auxiliaries against the most powerful pre-Columbian empire in [[Mesoamerica]], which was ruled by [[Moctezuma II]]. The empire's downfall followed from European weaponry, alliances with rebellious Indigenous populations and European diseases. A first wave of [[Smallpox|smallpox]] in 1520 killed an estimated 5–8 million people. The final victory came on 13 August 1521, when Spanish and Tlaxcalan forces captured the Aztec emperor Cuauhtémoc and the capital, [[Tenochtitlan]]. Its fall established [[New Spain]], part of the [[Spanish Empire]], with its capital at [[Mexico City]], built on the ruins of the former capital.

headword: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire
sort_key: spanish conquest of the inca empire
entry: Campaign by which Spain conquered the [[Inca Empire]] in South America, 1532–1572. In 1532, 168 Spanish soldiers under [[Francisco Pizarro]] and their Indigenous auxiliaries captured the last Sapa Inca, [[Atahualpa]], at the Battle of Cajamarca. The campaign took decades of fighting and ended with Spanish victory in 1572 and colonization of the region as the [[Peru|Viceroyalty of Peru]]. Spin-off campaigns reached present-day [[Chile]] and [[Colombia]], and expeditions went into the Amazon Basin. The empire had grown from about 400,000 sq km in 1448 to 1,800,000 sq km by 1528, and scholars estimate its population at between 12 and 16 million. Huayna Capac and his heir died suddenly in 1528, probably of [[Smallpox|smallpox]], a disease introduced by the Spanish into the Americas, and a civil war between the princes Huáscar and Atahualpa followed that greatly aided the Spanish.

Exceptionally deadly global [[Influenza|influenza]] pandemic of 1918–1920, caused by the H1N1 subtype of influenza A virus. The earliest probable cases were documented in March 1918 in Haskell County, [[Kansas]]. Two years later, nearly a third of the global population, an estimated 500 million people, had been infected. Estimates of deaths range from 17 million to 50 million, and possibly as high as 100 million. The pandemic broke out near the end of [[World War I]], when wartime [[Censorship|censors]] suppressed bad news, but newspapers freely reported the outbreak in neutral [[Spain]], creating a misleading impression of Spain as the epicenter and leading to the name Spanish flu. Most influenza outbreaks kill mainly the young and old, but this pandemic had unusually high mortality among young adults, a claim that has been contested. World War I worsened malnourishment, overcrowding and poor [[Hygiene|hygiene]], promoting bacterial superinfection that killed most victims after a typically prolonged death bed.

Literature written in Spanish within the territory of present-day [[Spain]]. Its development intersected with Catalan and Galician literature and with Latin, Jewish and Arabic traditions of the [[Iberian Peninsula]]. The [[Epic poetry|epic poem]] *Cantar de Mio Cid*, composed between 1140 and 1207, is among its earliest notable works. [[Prose|Spanish prose]] gained popularity in the mid-13th century, and in the 16th century the first Spanish [[Novel|novels]], *Lazarillo de Tormes* and *Guzmán de Alfarache*, appeared. In the Baroque era of the 17th century, [[Miguel de Cervantes]] wrote *Don Quixote de la Mancha*, a novel that consolidated the picaresque form into a template for later fiction. Enlightenment, Romantic and Realist writers followed, and [[Modernism]] produced several currents, including [[Futurism]]. The literature of Spanish America is an important branch, with its own characteristics dating back to the earliest years of Spain's conquest of the Americas.

Epiphytic [[Flowering plant|flowering plant]] (*Tillandsia usneoides*) of the [[Bromeliaceae|bromeliad]] family, often growing on large trees in tropical and subtropical climates. It is native to much of [[Mexico]], Bermuda, the Bahamas, Central America, South America and the Southern United States, and it has been naturalized in Queensland, Australia. It has the widest distribution of any bromeliad. In the United States it is common on southern live oak and bald cypress in lowland swamps and marshes from southeastern [[Virginia]] to [[Florida]] and west to southern Arkansas and Texas. Although it resembles the [[Lichen|lichen]] *Usnea*, it is neither a lichen nor a moss, and it is not native to [[Spain]]. The plant has no roots and is not parasitic, absorbing nutrients and water through its leaves from air and rain.

Ancient Greek city-state (polis) in Laconia, in the southeastern Peloponnese. From the 7th century BC it was the most prominent land military power in the Greek world, a status it kept until its defeat at Leuctra in 371 BC. In the 6th century BC it founded the Peloponnesian League, and its army was crucial at Thermopylae and Plataea during the second Persian invasion. Sparta led the League against the [[Athens|Athenian Empire]] in the [[Peloponnesian War]] (431–404 BC) and emerged victorious. Its social system, supposedly introduced by the semi-mythical lawgiver [[Lycurgus]], was exceptionally militarized: full citizens, the Spartiates, trained under the harsh agoge, while helots, enslaved non-Spartan locals, made up the vast majority of the population and repeatedly revolted. Sparta was sacked in 396 AD by the Visigothic king Alaric and declined into the medieval period, when much of its population moved to nearby Mystras.

Thracian gladiator and escaped slave leader of the Third Servile War, a major slave uprising against the [[Roman Republic]]. The main accounts of his life, by [[Plutarch]] and Appian, were written more than a century later and are contradictory. He came from near the Strymon River in Thrace, possibly of the Maedi tribe, and had served as a Roman soldier before being enslaved as a [[Gladiator|gladiator]]. In 73 BC he and about 70 other gladiators escaped a gladiatorial school near Capua, and his forces swelled to an estimated 70,000 enslaved people and others. After initial successes and attempts to negotiate and to escape to [[Sicily]], his army was defeated in 71 BC by [[Marcus Licinius Crassus]], who had been tasked with suppressing the revolt. Spartacus was presumed killed, though his body was never found, and about 6,000 captured rebels were crucified along the Appian Way.

1960 American epic historical drama film directed by [[Stanley Kubrick]] and starring [[Kirk Douglas]] as a slave and gladiator who leads a rebellion against Rome. Adapted by Dalton Trumbo from Howard Fast's 1951 novel, it was the only Kubrick film in which he lacked complete artistic control. Douglas publicly credited the blacklisted Trumbo as screenwriter, and President [[John F. Kennedy]] crossed picket lines to see it. The film won four [[Academy Awards]] from six nominations and was the highest-grossing film in [[Universal Pictures]] history at its release. In 2017 it was selected for the United States National Film Registry.

Polearm consisting of a usually wooden shaft with a pointed head, which may be the sharpened shaft itself or a durable material such as [[Flint|flint]], bone, obsidian, copper, [[Bronze|bronze]], [[Iron|iron]] or steel. Spears are designed either for thrusting, as with lances and pikes, or for throwing, as with javelins. People have used them for at least 400,000 years for hunting, fishing and warfare, and they are among the earliest and most widespread tools, along with the club, [[Knife|knife]] and [[Axe|axe]]. Wooden spears found at Clacton in England and Schöningen in Germany are at least 400,000 years old, and by 15,000 BC hunters used wooden and bone spear-launchers. Spears were used in virtually every conflict until the [[Modern era|modern era]], and they survive as the [[Bayonet|bayonet]] fixed to the muzzle of a long gun. Western chimpanzees in Senegal have been observed making spears to hunt [[Galago|galagos]].

Illusions or visual tricks used in the [[Theatre|theater]], [[Film|film]], [[Television]], [[Video game|video game]], [[Amusement park|amusement park]] and simulator industries to simulate fictional events. Special effects are traditionally divided into mechanical effects, also called practical effects, and optical effects, also called photographic effects. Mechanical effects, such as animatronics, pyrotechnics and [[Scale model|scale models]], are usually accomplished during live-action shooting. Optical effects use multiple exposure, mattes or an optical printer. In 1895 Alfred Clark created what is commonly accepted as the first motion picture special effect, replacing an actor with a dummy during a re-enactment of the beheading of [[Mary, Queen of Scots]]. [[Georges Méliès]] later made more than 500 short films between 1896 and 1914, developing techniques such as multiple exposures, time-lapse photography and dissolves. Since the 1990s, computer-generated imagery (CGI) has come to the forefront, and many optical and mechanical techniques have been superseded by CGI.

Scientific theory of the relationship between space and time, presented by [[Albert Einstein]] in his 1905 paper "On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies." It rests on two postulates: that the laws of physics are identical in all inertial frames of reference, a principle first formulated by [[Galileo Galilei]], and that the [[Speed of light|speed of light]] in vacuum is the same for all observers, regardless of the motion of the light source or observer. It replaces the idea of a single time flowing equally everywhere with the concept that time flows differently for each independent object. Consequences include [[Time dilation|time dilation]], length contraction and the relativity of simultaneity. Combined with other laws of physics, it predicts the [[Mass–energy equivalence|equivalence of mass and energy]], expressed as E = mc², where c is the speed of light in vacuum. The theory was extended to include gravity in 1916, in [[General relativity|general relativity]].

Heat that must be added to one unit of mass of a substance to raise its temperature by one unit. Its SI unit is joule per kelvin per kilogram (J⋅kg⁻¹⋅K⁻¹). The specific heat of [[Water|water]] is 4184 J⋅kg⁻¹⋅K⁻¹ at 20 °C, while that of [[Iron|iron]] is about 449 J⋅kg⁻¹⋅K⁻¹ and that of hydrogen gas is 14300 J⋅kg⁻¹⋅K⁻¹. It varies with [[Temperature|temperature]], and it is technically undefined during a [[Phase transition|phase transition]] such as melting or boiling.

Bear species native to the [[Andes]] of northern and western [[South America]], also called the Andean bear. It is the only living bear native to South America and the last surviving short-faced bear, subfamily Tremarctinae, whose relatives included [[Arctodus]] and Arctotherium, which became extinct at the end of the [[Pleistocene]] around 12,000 years ago. Its diet is mostly herbivorous, unlike that of other omnivorous bears. Its name refers to the light markings on its chest, neck and face, which may resemble spectacles. The IUCN lists it as vulnerable because of habitat loss.

Scientific instrument used to separate and measure the spectral components of a physical phenomenon. In visible light, a spectrometer separates white light into narrow bands of color, called a spectrum, using a [[Prism (optics)|prism]] or a [[Diffraction grating|diffraction grating]]. A mass spectrometer measures the spectrum of the masses of atoms or molecules in a gas, identifying the amount and type of chemicals in a sample by their mass-to-charge ratio and the abundance of gas-phase [[Ion|ions]]. Spectrometers are used in [[Astronomy|astronomy]] to analyze the chemical composition of stars and planets, and in [[Chemistry|chemistry]] and [[Particle physics|particle physics]] to separate particles, atoms and molecules by their mass, momentum or energy. Optical emission spectrometers evaluate [[Metal|metals]] to determine their chemical composition with very high accuracy.

Field of study that measures and interprets electromagnetic spectra as they interact with matter. It is a fundamental exploratory tool in [[Astronomy|astronomy]], [[Chemistry|chemistry]], [[Materials science|materials science]] and [[Physics|physics]], allowing the composition and structure of matter to be investigated from the atomic scale to astronomical distances. Spectroscopy began when [[Isaac Newton]] split light with a [[Prism (optics)|prism]], and [[James Clerk Maxwell]] later extended the field to the entire electromagnetic spectrum. Spectroscopic studies were central to the development of [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]], as early atomic models, including the Bohr model and the Schrödinger equation, reproduced the spectral lines of hydrogen. Current applications include biomedical spectroscopy in tissue analysis and medical imaging.

Utterance that not only presents information but also performs an action, as in the phrase "I resign," where saying the words enacts the resignation. The contemporary term goes back to J. L. Austin's work on performative utterances and his distinction among locutionary, illocutionary and perlocutionary acts. Acts commonly classed as speech acts include apologizing, promising, ordering, requesting, complaining, warning, inviting, refusing and congratulating. Kent Bach argued that almost any speech act is the performance of several acts at once, distinguished by the speaker's intention. The theory draws on Wittgenstein's view that meaning lies in use, and it is studied in [[Philosophy of language|philosophy of language]] and [[Linguistics|linguistics]].

Artificial production of human speech, carried out by a speech synthesizer in software or hardware. A text-to-speech (TTS) system converts ordinary text into speech in two stages: a front-end that turns symbols such as numbers and abbreviations into written-out words and assigns [[Phoneme|phonetic]] transcriptions, and a back-end that converts the result into sound. Synthesized speech may be made by concatenating recorded speech units stored in a [[Database|database]], or by modeling the vocal tract. The earliest [[Operating system|operating system]] to include a synthesizer was [[Unix]] in 1974, through its speak utility. Intelligible text-to-speech lets people with [[Visual impairment|visual impairments]] or reading disabilities hear written words. In the 1930s [[Bell Labs]] developed the vocoder, and in 1939 Homer Dudley's keyboard-operated Voder was exhibited at the New York World's Fair.

Magnitude of [[Velocity|velocity]], the rate at which the distance traveled by an object changes with time. Average speed is the total distance divided by the time interval, while instantaneous speed is the limit of average speed as the interval approaches zero. Speed has the dimensions of distance divided by time. Its SI unit is the [[Metre|meter]] per second (m/s), and the kilometer per hour, mile per hour and [[Knot (unit)|knot]] are also used. [[Galileo Galilei]] is usually credited with first measuring speed as the distance covered per unit of time. According to [[Special relativity|special relativity]], the fastest possible speed at which energy or information can travel is the [[Speed of light|speed of light]] in vacuum, c = 299,792,458 meters per second, and matter cannot reach it.

Distance a sound wave travels per unit of time through an elastic medium. At 20 °C (68 °F) it is about 343 m/s in air, and it depends strongly on temperature and on the medium. Sound travels most slowly in gases, faster in liquids and fastest in solids: about 1481 m/s in fresh [[Water|water]] at 20 °C, 5120 m/s in [[Iron|iron]] and 12,000 m/s in [[Diamond|diamond]]. The ratio of an object's speed to the speed of sound in the same medium is its [[Mach number]], and objects faster than the speed of sound travel at supersonic speeds. [[Isaac Newton]]'s 1687 calculation of the speed of sound in air was too low by about 15%, a discrepancy that [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]] later explained by treating sound waves as adiabatic.

Competitive form of [[Ice skating|ice skating]] in which skaters race a set distance. The main types are long-track, short-track and marathon speed skating, and at the [[Olympic Games]] long-track is usually called simply speed skating. Long-track races take place on a 400 m ice track and short-track races on a 111 m track. An international federation was founded in 1892, the first for any winter sport. The sport is especially popular in the [[Netherlands]], [[Norway]] and [[South Korea]], and has top rinks in Canada, the United States, Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia, Kazakhstan, China, Belarus and Poland. A World Cup circuit includes events in those countries and two in the Thialf ice hall in Heerenveen, Netherlands.

American actor known for his natural performing style. He was the first actor to win two consecutive [[Academy Awards]] for Best Actor, for *Captains Courageous* and *Boys Town*, from nine nominations. He appeared in 75 films and was one of [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer|MGM's]] top stars. His professional and personal partnership with [[Katharine Hepburn]] produced nine films over 25 years. He won the Best Actor prize at the [[Cannes Film Festival]] in 1955 for *Bad Day at Black Rock*. His last film, *Guess Who's Coming to Dinner*, was completed just 17 days before he died.

Male reproductive cell, or gamete, in the anisogamous forms of sexual reproduction, in which the male cell is smaller than the female. Sperm contribute approximately half of the nuclear genetic information to the diploid offspring, excluding in most cases mitochondrial DNA. Animal sperm are motile, with a [[Flagellum|flagellum]] tail, and are called spermatozoa, while [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] contain non-motile sperm inside [[Pollen|pollen]]. In amniotes such as [[Reptile|reptiles]] and [[Mammal|mammals]], sperm form through spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules of the testicles, a process that takes around 3 months. A human sperm cell is haploid, carrying 23 chromosomes that join the 23 of the egg to form a diploid cell with 46. In mammals, sperm is stored in the epididymis and released through the penis in [[Semen|semen]] during [[Ejaculation|ejaculation]]. The word sperm derives from the Greek *sperma*, meaning "seed."

Largest of the toothed whales and the largest toothed predator, the only living member of the genus *Physeter*. It is a pelagic [[Mammal|mammal]] with a worldwide range, and mature males average 16 meters (52 ft) in length. It dives to 2,250 meters (7,380 ft), the third deepest of any diving mammal, and its sounds can reach a source level of 236 decibels, the loudest of any animal. It has the largest brain on Earth, more than five times heavier than a human's. The head holds spermaceti, a waxy substance that gave the whale its name and was a prime target of the [[Whaling|whaling]] industry. Ambergris, a waxy waste product from the digestive system, is still highly valued as a fixative in [[Perfume|perfumes]]. Sperm whaling was a major industry in the 19th century, depicted in the novel *Moby-Dick*. The species is protected by the International Whaling Commission moratorium and is listed as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

Genus of approximately 380 species of mosses, also known as bog moss or sphagnum moss. Its plants can hold 16 to 26 times their dry weight in water. As it spreads into drier conditions it forms larger [[Bog|bogs]], both raised and blanket, and the peat accumulations provide habitat for sedges, orchids and carnivorous plants. Phenolic compounds in its cell walls make the moss and the [[Peat|peat]] it forms resistant to decay. By taking up [[Calcium|calcium]] and [[Magnesium|magnesium]] ions and releasing [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]] ions, it acidifies its surroundings. Peat can accumulate to a depth of many meters. Like all land plants, it alternates between generations, and its [[Gametophyte|gametophyte]] generation is dominant and long-lived.
